content_voiceover: This slide covers two questions about modern hemophilia treatment. The first asks fellows to spot the incorrect statement about severe hemophilia A management. Extended half-life clotting factor concentrates have genuinely reduced treatment burden, and population pharmacokinetic tools now support individualized prophylactic dosing, both true statements. The trap answer describes fitusiran as a licensed non-factor replacement therapy that mimics factor eight cofactor activity. In reality, fitusiran is a small interfering RNA therapeutic that lowers antithrombin, rebalancing hemostasis indirectly rather than mimicking factor eight, and importantly it is not yet a licensed, marketed product, so this statement is wrong on two counts. The PROPEL study and the ALTUVIIIO once weekly efanesoctocog alfa data are both accurately described and represent real, testable evidence in current hemophilia literature. The second question is a clinical vignette involving a boy with severe hemophilia B and a high responding inhibitor who develops a joint bleed while on long acting factor nine prophylaxis. Because he has an inhibitor against factor nine, simply giving more factor nine will not work. The correct emergency approach is a bypassing agent, specifically recombinant activated factor seven, rather than escalating factor nine dosing, switching factor products, or just observing with ice.
keypoints: Fitusiran is an antithrombin-lowering siRNA, not an FVIII mimetic, and not yet licensed
Extended half-life products and population PK dosing are established tools
ALTUVIIIO and PROPEL trial data reflect real evidence in current guidelines
High-responding FIX inhibitor plus bleed requires a bypassing agent, not more FIX
keypoint_voiceover: Two facts to lock in. Fitusiran works by silencing antithrombin production, it does not mimic factor eight, and it is still investigational rather than licensed. And when a hemophilia B patient with a high responding inhibitor bleeds, do not chase the dose with more factor nine, switch to a bypassing agent like recombinant activated factor seven instead.
